cls: Selective xanthine oxidase (xanthine oxidoreductase) inhibitor - non-purine
quick: Start 20 mg orally twice daily; titrate gradually to a usual 60 mg twice daily (max 80 mg twice daily)
May be taken with or without food, twice daily (morning and evening)
Not recommended; safety in pregnancy not established
Avoid; excreted in milk in animal studies
Can be used across renal function including moderate impairment; titrate to urate target
Monitor liver function; caution in hepatic impairment
Limit alcohol - it raises urate and may worsen liver effects
Serum urate, liver enzymes, and gout flares early in therapy
summary: Topiroxostat is a selective non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor used to treat hyperuricemia with or without gout. By blocking the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid it lowers serum urate. It was developed and approved in Japan (and used in some Asian markets) and is not FDA-approved. As with other urate-lowering drugs, gout flares can occur on initiation and liver enzymes should be monitored.
indications: Hyperuricemia, including hyperuricemia associated with gout (chronic urate-lowering therapy)

dosage.d: Increase gradually to 60 mg twice daily over several weeks
Usual 60 mg twice daily; maximum 80 mg twice daily

admin: Take twice daily (morning and evening), with or without food
Start at a low dose and titrate slowly to minimize gout flares
Consider flare prophylaxis (colchicine or NSAID) when starting
Continue long term to maintain target serum urate
moa: Topiroxostat is a selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase (xanthine oxidoreductase), the enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. It binds covalently/structurally to both the oxidized and reduced forms of the enzyme, producing potent, long-lasting inhibition and thereby lowering serum uric acid.

absolute: Concomitant mercaptopurine or azathioprine (markedly increased toxicity from blocked metabolism)
relative: Active acute gout flare (do not start during a flare; do not stop if a flare occurs once established)

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established and use is not recommended. Hyperuricemia/gout treatment is generally deferred in pregnancy; use only if clearly necessary under specialist advice.
lact: Topiroxostat or its metabolites were excreted in milk in animal studies; breastfeeding should be avoided during treatment.
renal: Topiroxostat is largely metabolized (glucuronidation/oxidation) rather than renally excreted unchanged, so it can be used across a range of renal function including moderate impairment; titrate to the serum urate target and monitor.
hepatic: Liver enzyme elevations can occur. Monitor liver function and use with caution in hepatic impairment.

major: Mercaptopurine and azathioprine (xanthine oxidase inhibition raises their levels - severe myelosuppression) - avoid
moderate: Other drugs metabolized by xanthine oxidase
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - raises serum urate and may add to hepatic effects
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum and urine xanthine/hypoxanthine; monitor liver transaminases

rare: Xanthine deposition/urolithiasis (theoretical, with very high urate turnover)

monitoring: Serum uric acid (titrate to target, commonly <6 mg/dL)
Liver function tests at baseline and periodically
counsel: Keep taking the medicine even if you get a gout attack - do not stop it once established
Gout flares are common when starting; your doctor may give a preventive medicine for the first months
Take it twice daily as prescribed and have your blood (urate and liver) checked
Tell your doctor if you take azathioprine or mercaptopurine - these must not be combined
pk: Urate begins to fall within days; full effect over weeks of dosing
Plasma peak roughly 1 hour after an oral dose
Short plasma half-life (a few hours) but prolonged enzyme inhibition supports twice-daily dosing
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture and light
pearls: A non-purine selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor in the same therapeutic class as febuxostat/allopurinol
Approved and used mainly in Japan (e.g., Topiloric/Uriadec) - NOT FDA-approved; dosing follows the Japanese package insert
Because it is metabolized rather than renally cleared, it is convenient in renal impairment
Like other urate-lowering agents, expect flares on initiation and use flare prophylaxis; never combine with azathioprine/mercaptopurine
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Effects would be expected to extend the pharmacologic action (urate lowering, possible liver enzyme elevation, xanthine accumulation). There is no specific antidote; manage supportively with hydration and monitoring of liver and renal function.
